https://www.dw.com/en/tech-giants-urge-g.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JXTU AI companies want more money and resources put towards cyberdefense Image: Philip Dulian/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement More than 100 companies, including AI giants OpenAI , Anthropic , Google and Perplexity, have signed an open letter calling for a global effort to strengthen AI-powered cybersecurity threats . "We have a limited window to strengthen cyber defenses," the letter read. "In the coming months, AI-enabled cyber attacks will become far more widespread and sophisticated as models around the world become increasingly capable." Other signatories to the open letter include Adobe, AMD, Cisco, Dell, Oracle, IBM and German tech giant SAP as well as Deutsche Telekom . Letter urges more funding, resources for cybersecurity The companies called for a broad response, ranging from end-user companies strengthening their own security protocols to "frontier AI companies" building new observability and security tools to cope with AI-powered threats. In particular, they also called on governments to pay for local and international responses to new threats to cybersecurity. "Fund cyber defense, starting with essential services that lack the staff or budget to act," the letter read. In the United States, the Trump administration has imposed deep cuts to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) last year, cutting staff by around a third. Is AI the new weapon of mass data theft? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The letter also urged governments to "expedite the expansion of trusted access programs, especially for critical infrastructure supply chains, and broaden access to defensive capabilities for other defenders." AI agents reportedly go rogue Last month, OpenAI said two of its models escaped their test environment , gained access to the internet and attacked Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code. The incident prompted Anthropic to check if its own models had also carried out similar attacks. It found three incidents in which a Claude model broke out of its testing environment and breached the systems of three organizations. In June, the "Five Eyes" intelligence community — consisting of the US, the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand — issued a rare joint statement warning that new AI models were "fundamentally transforming both offensive and defensive cyber capabilities." "The timeline is not years, it is months," the statement said. In this case, we cannot even speak of the ordinary level of public deception that exists in any society or political system. banner-Pro-Memoria.-960x540-1.jpg Steliu Lambru , 07.09.2026, 14:00 Through all its forms of expression, communist lying reached its highest possible limits. What made these lies so powerful was the fear they generated: they could not be openly contradicted without exposing the individual to major risks for their freedom, their life, and the safety of those close to them. Communist lies were crude and aggressive, blatantly contradicting reality. And the lies about economic performance and the standard of living were no exception. In fact, deception about the economy and living conditions was a natural consequence of the general lack of freedom. One of the obsessions of communist ideology was the centrally planned economy, and one of its enemies was economic freedom. From grossly manipulated statistics and triumphant declarations about the country’s accelerated development to the denial of the desperate economic situation and the shortages in which Romanians struggled, lies about the economy and living standards covered the entire spectrum. Ultimately, the generalized economic crisis of communist regimes was what led to their collapse in 1989. Paradoxically, social memory has preserved the lies of the communist regime even in democracy, once society became free again. In today’s Romania, the same pre 1989 falsehoods continue to circulate, a practice found in all former communist societies. Historian Cosmin Popa of the “Nicolae Iorga” Institute of the Romanian Academy, author of studies and volumes on the economy of the Romanian communist regime, explains the paradox of the survival of communist lies, embraced even by new generations born after its fall. Cosmin Popa: “It would be very easy to say how lying worked under communism: everyone lied. But I don’t think that would help us understand why communist lies persist today, why they are stronger than ever, and why they continue to shape society and public morality. So I focused my efforts on understanding rationalization, because I noticed that we are dealing with a cumulative mechanism of lying. It is a radicalization of the lie. There is a historian, Hans Mommsen, who wrote extensively about the Holocaust and who speaks of a cumulative radicalization of the decision that led to the Holocaust. It began with an idea and, through radicalization and interaction with external events, reached the final decision as it was fixed in the second half of 1942. The same thing happens in communism.” Cosmin Popa also identified what made the Ceaușescu regime even more repellent in terms of public deception: “Communism is an ideology condemned to success, condemned to progress. But what makes Romanian communism particularly distinctive is that it always managed to avoid the dilemma of self reflection. One scenario would have been to stop and examine what had happened. The second scenario, which Romanian communists chose, was to adopt the strategy of infallibility: we did everything right. Everything that went wrong had to be blamed on external forces, on outdated, dead, or dismissed figures. But generally, failure was attributed to outside influence. This strategy of infallibility allowed something fundamental: it greatly slowed down the emergence of anti communist sentiment in society. The regime moved from lie to lie, each more radical than the last, within this cumulative mechanism, until society itself came to accept the regime, to live in a kind of organic complicity with it. This explains, in many ways, the sudden success that followed after 1989.” Cosmin Popa identified seven types of pre 1989 lies that continue to thrive today, both among older nostalgic generations and among younger, more intellectual ones: the lie of Romanian economic independence, the lie of Westernization and liberalization of the regime, the lie of economic modernization, the lie of egalitarianism, the lie of intellectuals’ collaboration with the regime, the lie of recovering bourgeois cultural values, and the lie of the “good Ceaușescu” surrounded by a harmful entourage. To these we can add others, such as the lie of the patriotic Securitate, the repressive apparatus. Of the seven types of lies, at least four are related to the economy. Popa emphasized that these lies generated a fundamental element of individual and societal behavior in communist Romania, one that post communist Romania inherited. Cosmin Popa: “Thus, an industry of lying was created, to which corruption was added. Why? Because propaganda alone is not enough; propaganda together with repression is not sufficient to make such a society function. Something else is needed, one more ingredient that makes this society acceptable and makes the lie acceptable to those who live within it. And that ingredient is corruption. This corruption gives the society the strength to function, creates value systems, shapes public morality, and ultimately creates a kind of natural symbiosis between the regime and society.” But the lies of communist Romania can no longer deceive, even if they are fashionable today; they remain what they always were. Because truth is always stronger and eventually comes to the surface. https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-new.text: As the US House of Representatives cleared a bill posing a threat of up to 100% tariffs on India, China and other countries, a senator backed the proposal, saying a “strong message” was needed for countries buying Russian oil. “We need to send a very strong message, not just to Vladimir Putin, but to anybody who is buying Russian oil and gas, that they are going to pay a price for that,” said Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen on Thursday after the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 bill cleared the House.The act, which will grant the Trump administration the authority to place tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the five top purchasers of Russian oil and gas, was passed in the US House of Representatives by a 262-159 margin. The bill, which is likely to target India, China, Slovakia, Hungary and Azerbaijan, will now head to President Donald Trump’s desk to be signed into law. ‘Russian oil going to India, China’Shaheen backed the bill, accusing Russia of fighting its war against Ukraine, from revenue earned by selling oil and gas to India and China, among others, at less than market rates.“Russia is funding its war in Ukraine with revenues from oil and gas. And they're getting that oil and gas sold by using the shadow fleet, which means that it's being bought at less-than-market rates. And it's going mostly to countries like China and India,” she said in an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper.Also Read: How US bill proposing 100% tariffs over Russian oil purchase could hurt India“Every dollar Russia earns through illicit energy sales is another dollar Putin can use to buy drones, missiles and weapons to kill innocent Ukrainians. This bill will help cut off that revenue, force Putin to the negotiating table by increasing pressure on Moscow and strengthen Ukraine’s hand as it fights for its survival,” she said in a statement released after the House vote.She added that the bill will send a message to not only Russian President Vladimir Putin, but to countries who purchase oil and gas from the country, stressing that China was the top user of Russian oil and gas.“China is the top user of Russian oil and gas. And we need to send a very strong message, not just to Vladimir Putin, but to China and to anybody who is buying Russian oil and gas, that they are going to pay a price for that, because they are facilitating Russia's unprovoked and horrific war in Ukraine.” ‘Need to send a message to Ukrainians’Shaheen said a message also needed to be sent to Ukrainians, whom she described as undertaking a “heroic effort” despite what she called “terrible Russian attacks,” saying there is bipartisan support in Congress for their efforts.“We also need to send a message to the Ukrainians that there is bipartisan support in Congress for the heroic effort that they are continuing to undertake every day against terrible Russian attacks. So this is a very important bill that puts the United States in line with our European allies.”“Lindsey Graham understood that Putin only responds to pressure, and he worked tirelessly to get this legislation to this point. There could be no more fitting tribute to Lindsey and his commitment to a free and secure Ukraine than seeing this bill signed into law,” the statement added. What is the Russia sanctions act?The bill - officially known as the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 had already passed by an overwhelming margin in the Senate, which means it will now head to President Donald Trump’s desk to be signed into law.After escaping a bleak chance of being passed in the House last week amid divisions between both the Republican and opposition Democratic party about handing President Trump greater authority to levy tariffs ahead of November’s crucial midterm elections., the act gained momentum in the House on Wednesday and was passed narrowly by a 214-211 margin after two Democratic lawmakers unexpectedly crossed the aisle to vote alongside the majority Republican party.It is important to note that the Russia sanctions bill does not compel President Trump to place tariffs on countries purchasing oil and gas from Russia. It also includes substantial exemptions for America’s European allies, on the grounds that several of those nations have made efforts to reduce energy purchases from Russia.The Trump White House’s role in securing the passage of this bill remains unclear. However, recent reports in the US media indicate the White House may have played a key role in pushing for the bill by inducing lawmakers from the opposition Democratic party to vote for the legislation.India-Russia tiesMore recently, Russia’s Ambassador to Delhi, Denis Alipov, said that Russia stands ready to supply India with "as much oil as it needs." His comments came against the backdrop of tariff threats from the Trump administration.Speaking to news agency ANI, the Russian envoy slammed the "pressure tactics" by the US and stated that Moscow remains ready to continue sales with India.“We would be ready to supply as much oil as India needs. Unfortunately, those who impose sanctions and tariffs have taken the path of pressure tactics instead of honest cooperation, which prevents those countries from offering a better deal to India in oil than us," the envoy told ANI.Exactly a year earlier, the US penalised India over its energy trade with Russia when President Donald Trump announced an additional 25 per cent tariff against India for "fueling Putin's war". However, as the US' war with Iran saw closure of the crucial waterway Strait of Hormuz, Washington revoked the waiver to ease the effect of rising oil prices across the globe. How will the bill impact India Since the war in the West Asia broke out in February this year, India's dependence on Russian energy has increased as the shipping route via the crucial Strait of Hormuz passage remained disrupted. The Iran-US war has choked off Gulf crude supplies that previously accounted for roughly 40% of India’s oil imports, forcing refiners to turn to Russian crude as an alternative source. Amid the waiver, Indian imports of Russian crude oil rose 34% in June 2026 to record levels. According to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, these imports were valued at €4.5 billion, accounting for roughly 36% of Russia’s crude oil export revenues.

Photograph: Social Media/Reuters View image in fullscreen Smoke billows from the presidential palace following an attack by the Houthis, according to government officials, in Aden, Yemen, on Thursday. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters Yemen Houthi missiles strike Saudi-led forces HQ at presidential palace in Aden Witnesses report at least six explosions near palace used by Yemen's internationally recognized government Guardian staff and agencies Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 16.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by Yemen ’s internationally recognized government in the port city of Aden, witnesses said. An official told the Associated Press that at least two people were killed, and Iran -backed Houthi rebels based in northern Yemen quickly claimed responsibility. Government military sources in Yemen told Agence-France Press (AFP) that at least four people were killed and 10 wounded. An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July. A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Yemeni prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”. It was a rare attack on the palace area, as fighting has escalated between the rebels and a Saudi-led coalition on the latest front in the Iran war. The explosions caused panic among residents, who fled the area. At least two people were killed and six wounded, said the official, who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The government said the Houthis attacked with missiles and drones, the Aden-based Saba news agency reported. A security official told the AP that at least two explosions were on top of the hill near Al-Maashiq palace, and two others were near the security gate. AFP also reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity on Thursday that a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden had hit a command center for the Saudi-led coalition. The official added that the command center was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll. Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough Read more There was no immediate confirmation of the report that the prime minister was in the presidential palace at the time of Houthi attack. Many of Yemen’s government leaders are living in exile, and those in Aden were safe, a government official told the AP. The Houthis said they attacked a military operations headquarters with the “Saudi enemy”, part of their strategy of attacking Saudi targets that has included a series of attacks on airports and oil infrastructure inside the kingdom. The escalation has complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia , one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks. Regional aviation is affected, too, as the rebels have warned airlines about their use of Saudi airspace for attacks. Thousands of flights across the kingdom have been disrupted. Earlier on Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina. Flightradar24, a tracking platform, said dozens of flights were canceled or delayed at Jeddah’s airport. The coalition statement did not assign blame for the attack. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, denied the rebels carried it out. The group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over the country’s eastern province, a major oil-producing region, and intercepted a drone in Khamis Mushait, near a major military airbase. Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia said the headquarters of the oil giant Saudi Aramco were hit by Houthi attacks , and reported damage to the building. Inside Yemen, the fighting has revived a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm. One focus of alarm is the Houthi-besieged city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where residents were running short of basic necessities.
